analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $6.65 and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 152 House members, never received a vote; it sat in committee from its February 2001 referral until Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in three steps — to $5.75 an hour 30 days after passage, $6.25 in 2002, and $6.65 in 2003 — from the then-current $5.15. It would also apply federal minimum wage law to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, a U.S. territory that was exempt, phasing its local minimum up 50 cents every six months until it matched the federal wage. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum — heavily concentrated in restaurants, retail, hotels, and care work — would get raises of up to $1.50 an hour, about $3,120 a year for a full-time worker at the final rate. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, where the local minimum was far below the federal one, would see their wage climb toward the federal standard over several years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.75 within 30 days of enactment, then to $6.25 on January 1, 2002, and $6.65 on January 1, 2003.

Applies the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, starting at $3.55 there and rising 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal rate.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail chains, hotels, and nursing and care providers — would bear higher payroll costs. In the Northern Mariana Islands, garment factories and tourism businesses that had relied on the exemption would face a phased-in federal wage for the first time. Some of the cost could be passed to consumers through prices, and some low-wage positions could be cut or hours reduced.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retailers, hotels, and CNMI employers

drawbacks.text: The wage floor was modest by the standards of the decade: $6.65 by 2003 would have left the inflation-adjusted minimum wage lower than it had been in the late 1960s, so the bill was a partial fix rather than a full one.

Critics of minimum wage increases argue that mandated raises raise costs for small businesses and can lead to reduced hours or fewer entry-level jobs, and that the burden falls hardest on restaurants and small retailers operating on thin margins.
Extending the federal wage to the Northern Mariana Islands, even with a transition, risked pressuring its garment industry, which competed on low labor costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and easy to see: a raise for the country's lowest-paid workers, funded mostly by the employers who pay them. The main honest objection is the standard one — that a higher floor can price out some entry-level jobs and squeeze small employers — and the strongest version of that argument applies to abrupt increases, not to the two-year step-in this bill used. The CNMI provision carried a real adjustment risk for that territory's industries but closed a long-standing hole in the wage floor. On balance the costs were modest and targeted while the gains went to millions of workers; the bill's failure was a choice not to raise the floor, not a discovered flaw in the design.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Education and the Workforce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee in April 2001, and it never came up again before Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: David Bonior introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2001 on February 14, 2001, with 152 cosponsors — 151 of the chamber's 208 Democrats plus the chamber's one Independent — signed on at introduction.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On April 5, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last recorded action in its two-year life.
The committee never reported the bill, no committee or floor vote was ever held, and no companion Senate action appears in the record; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers — especially large restaurant, retail, and hotel companies — avoided a $1.50-an-hour increase, and businesses in the Northern Mariana Islands kept their exemption from the federal wage floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers and Northern Mariana businesses

for.name: David E. Bonior
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2001 and recruited 152 original cosponsors.

for.name: 151 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill when it was introduced, giving it the support of nearly three-quarters of the House Democratic caucus from day one.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Representative (VT), the chamber's sole Independent

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for wage and labor bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in February 2001 and never reported it out; the bill's last recorded action was a subcommittee referral in April 2001.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled which bills reached the floor
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 152 cosponsors was a Democrat or the chamber's single Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-held committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: These businesses would have had to raise pay for their lowest-wage employees, the direct cost of the bill. Their interest in stopping it ran against the workers who would have received the raise.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and tourism industry
industries.note: The bill would have ended the territory's exemption from federal minimum wage law, phasing in a much higher wage floor for its garment factories and hotels. These industries had benefited from paying below the federal minimum, a cost borne by their own workers.
